title: Point Slider
description: Count the zeros underneath, walk the point in from the right, and fill the empty places on the left when the digits run out.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; Hint, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded card holding the question bar with its Answer key, the running count, the working area (the whole card until Answer is tapped) and the answer panel that slides in from the right; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it, the phase dots and the phase and question counts at the right.

zones.layout: board: the question and the Answer key in a bar on top; the working area is the whole card until the child taps Answer, when the answer box and keypad slide in from the right and the area narrows to 1086
zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: Hint (data-control again), sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one pill per phase across bar, pitch 158; in user mode each is a button with a 72-tall finger box

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Turn a fraction into a decimal by counting the zeros underneath, and find out which side the filling zeros go on when the digits run out.
writeup.look: A fraction at the top with its denominator lit, the numerator laid out in digit cards below it, and a second lane under that running the other way.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Point Slider' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the fractions turned against the fractions this phase lays out, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each decimal is read back and the second fixed at however many this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The fraction stands at the top left of the working area, 300 by 140 at 64,206, its bar drawn near-black, its numerator above and its denominator below with the denominator lit. The zero counter sits beside it, 260 by 76 at 400,230: it counts the zeros of the denominator one at a time, lighting each zero in the denominator as it is counted, and writes the number of decimal places it has found, which is the only number it ever shows. The digit cards lie in a row across the middle of the working area at 300,370, each 96 by 116, one digit to a card, laid out from the numerator with no gaps between them. The point card is a narrower card 56 by 116 in vermilion and it waits just past their right hand end; it slides leftwards one whole digit at a time, the counter tracking each step, and it cannot be dropped until it has moved as many digits as the counter is holding. Where the digits run out before the count is met, the places still empty are drawn as outlined card spaces and lit BETWEEN the point card and the digits already there, that is on the LEFT of those digits, and a short arrow is drawn running inward from the point to the nearest empty one. The zero tray stands under the row at 300,500, offering grey zeros; a zero dropped into a lit empty place settles at the same size and weight as every other card, and a zero dropped past the right hand end of the digits is refused and springs back with nothing marked, the empty places on the left lit again and the arrow redrawn running inward from the point. The wrong side lane runs at 64,530, 1080 by 120: it loads the same fraction, hangs the zeros past the right hand end instead, walks its own point card in from the right of what that built, and carries the working all the way to a finished answer. The distance bar is drawn at 64,662, 1080 by 60, between the two answers, with how many times apart they are written along it. Neither lane is marked, neither is cleared, and the bar measures rather than judges. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever an answer is asked for, with a point key beside them and, under those, a zero key drawn grey that can only be pressed while a place on the left is lit and waiting, so that the pad and the tray agree about which side a filling zero goes on. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a digit standing to the left of the point is deep blue, a digit standing to the right of it is green, and the point itself is vermilion between them on every phase without exception. A part or a column standing for tenths is amber, one standing for hundredths is rose, one standing for thousandths is sky blue, and a zero that is only holding a place open is grey, whether it was written in on the left of a short numerator or printed on the end of a measurement. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every one of the readings survives with the colour taken away, because a place is told by the heading written over it before it is ever told by a colour, a filling zero is told by the short arrow running inward from the point, and a zero printed on the end is told by the place counter that lights it. Grey never means faint: such a zero is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. The arrow that marks a filling zero always runs inward, from the point towards the digits, and it is never drawn running the other way on any phase of this tool, including inside the wrong side lane, where the zeros are hung past the right hand end with no arrow drawn at all. The direction of that arrow is the whole of the teaching and it is never used for decoration.
writeup.finish: The card shows the fraction the child converted, its decimal with the places counted from the point, and any zeros they filled standing in front of the digits.

phases.win: the counter settles and that many empty places are drawn to the right of a point
phases.does: counts the zeros underneath and sets the counter to that many places
phases.goal: the zeros in the denominator count the decimal places
phases.says: Count the zeros underneath. That is how many places you need.
phases.check: Away from the screen: how many decimal places does a bottom number of a thousand ask for, and how do you know?
phases.feels: the bottom number is doing the deciding, and only its zeros are being counted
phases.hands: Write three fractions on the board with ten, a hundred and a thousand underneath them, and have the class count the zeros aloud and write only that count down, with nothing else attempted yet. Then draw that many empty boxes to the right of a point for each one. Ask what would change if the bottom number were ten thousand, and let them answer by counting rather than by rule.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which of the two numbers is the bottom one? Second rung, the phase's: how many zeros has it got? Third rung: the fraction is cut to a denominator of ten and the child counts it and draws the places. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: a hundred plainly has three digits and the count of digits is the easier thing to see, and for a denominator of ten the two counts are only one apart.
wrong.move: counts the digits of the denominator instead of its zeros, so a hundred asks for three decimal places.
wrong.screen: the counter runs again slowly with each zero of the denominator lighting as it is counted and the leading one left plain and uncounted, and the number it finds is written beside the child's count rather than over it. That many empty places are then drawn to the right of a point, and the child's count is drawn as a second row of places underneath, one longer.

wrong.why: the numerator is where the cards are laid out and where everything else is about to happen, so it is where the eye already is.
wrong.move: counts the zeros of the numerator, or its digits, because the top number is the one being worked on.
wrong.screen: the denominator lights on its own with the bar drawn heavier between the two, and the counter is walked across from the top number to the bottom one along a drawn path before it counts. The child's count stays written beside the counter, the numerator is dimmed to nothing but its outline while the counting runs, and both numbers stay on the stage afterwards.

phases.screen: a fraction at the top with its denominator lit and the counter still empty
phases.soWhat: The zeros in the denominator count the decimal places, one place for each zero.

phases.win: the point drops on the counted digit and the decimal is read back from the point outwards
phases.does: slides the point card leftwards one digit at a time until the count is met
phases.goal: the point goes in from the right hand end of the numerator
phases.says: Start at the right hand end and walk the point in. Count as you go.
phases.check: Turn a three digit numerator over a thousand into a decimal, and say which end you started counting from.
phases.feels: the walk starts at the right hand end every time, and the counting is what stops it
phases.hands: Give each group a fraction card and the loose digits of its numerator, laid out in a row on the desk with a card marked with a point beside them. They count the zeros below, then slide the point card in from the right hand end, one digit at a time, counting out loud as it goes. Then ask what they would have got by starting from the other end, and let one group try it and read the answer out.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many places does the counter say? Second rung, the phase's: which end does the point card start from? Third rung: the row is cut to two digit cards and the child walks the point in on them. The number pad and the point key stay open.

wrong.why: reading and counting both start at the left in everything else, and the left hand end of the row is where a hand naturally lands.
wrong.move: counts the point in from the LEFT hand end of the numerator, so a three digit numerator over a thousand comes out ten times too big.
wrong.screen: both walks are run on the same row of cards with both points left standing where they were dropped, one counted from the left and one from the right, and each answer is read back with its places counted outward from its own point. The leading digit of the child's answer is lit in the ones column, where it is standing for whole ones, and the two answers stay on the stage together.

wrong.why: several answers in a row with one digit in front of the point make a shape that is easy to copy, and copying a shape is faster than counting.
wrong.move: drops the point after the first digit every time, because the first few answers happened to come out looking like that.
wrong.screen: the counter is read out again and the point card is sent back to the right hand end and walked in with each step numbered above the card it passes, and it will not drop until the count is met. The child's point stays drawn where it was put, a second row of cards is laid underneath with the counted point in it, and both rows are read back from their own points outwards.

phases.screen: the numerator laid out in digit cards with the point card at its right hand end
phases.soWhat: The point goes in from the right hand end of the numerator, one digit for each zero underneath.
phases.concept: Placing the point from the right

phases.win: the zeros settle in front of the digits and every place is filled from the point outwards
phases.does: takes zeros from the tray and fills the empty places on the left
phases.goal: the filling zeros go on the left of the digits, between them and the point
phases.says: The digits have run out. Which side are the empty places on?
phases.check: Turn three over a hundred into a decimal. Where did the filling zero go, and which side of the digits is that?
phases.feels: the gap is always on the side nearest the point, so that is the side the zeros go in on
phases.hands: Hand each group a fraction whose numerator is shorter than the zeros underneath call for, with loose digit cards and loose zero cards. Lay the digits from the right hand end, then look at where the gap is. Say the direction out loud together and make the class say it back: the filling zeros go on the LEFT of the digits, between them and the point, because the places still empty are the ones nearest the point.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many places are still empty? Second rung, the phase's: which side of the digits are they on? Third rung: the row is cut to one digit card over a hundred and the child fills the one empty place. The grey zero key stays open.

wrong.why: the printed rule on the page sends the zeros to the right of the numerator. That is the wrong side and it is never what the worked example printed under it does: that example places a zero before the nine, two zeros before the four and a zero before the sixty-five, and says the word before all three times.
wrong.move: hangs the filling zeros on the right hand end of the digits, so nine hundredths is built out of nine hundred.
wrong.screen: the child's zeros stay hanging exactly where they were hung and the row is read out as the number it now is, which is nine hundred rather than nine. The empty places are then lit again between the point and the digits, on their left, with the short arrow drawn running inward from the point, and a second row is laid underneath with the grey zeros walked into those places instead. Both rows stay standing.

wrong.why: the digits that were given have all been used and the row looks finished, and a place with nothing in it does not look like a place at all.
wrong.move: lays the short numerator down and drops the point without filling anything, so three over a hundred comes out as three tenths.
wrong.screen: the counter is read out again against the row, and the empty place nearest the point is drawn and held lit with the arrow running inward to it, so that the number of places the answer actually has can be counted off against the number the counter is holding. The child's answer stays written, a grey zero is offered from the tray, and both answers are read back with their places counted outward from the point.

phases.screen: a short numerator with places still empty between it and the point
phases.soWhat: A filling zero goes on the left of the digits, between them and the point, and never on their right hand end.
phases.concept: When the numerator is too short

phases.win: both answers stand together and the distance bar says how many times out the wrong one is
phases.does: runs the wrong side lane to its answer and measures the gap between the two
phases.goal: zeros on the wrong side make the number bigger instead of smaller
phases.says: Try it the other way and see where it lands. How far apart are they?
phases.check: A child turns four over a thousand into a decimal by hanging the zeros on the right hand end instead of on the left, in front of the four. How far out is the answer?
phases.feels: the wrong side does not look wrong, it looks finished, and that is exactly what makes it worth measuring
phases.hands: Run the wrong side once, in public, all the way to its answer, so that it is never a mystery afterwards. Write nine hundredths properly on one line and then, underneath, hang the zeros on the right of the nine and carry that working through to its end. Put the two answers side by side and ask how far apart they are. Then do the same with four over a thousand and let the class say which of the two mistakes cost more.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what did the second lane come out with? Second rung, the phase's: is that bigger or smaller than the fraction asked for? Third rung: both lanes are cut to a single digit numerator over a hundred and the child runs them side by side. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: every step of that lane really was carried out properly, and a tidy answer at the end of careful work is hard to doubt.
wrong.move: takes the second lane's answer as the right one, because it came out a tidy whole number and the working was done carefully.
wrong.screen: both answers are carried down to the grid and the strip and drawn at their real sizes, one as a few cells of a hundred and the other as nine whole ones laid out along the stage, so the two are seen rather than compared on the line. The distance bar writes how many times apart they are, both answers stay standing where they were made, and nothing is marked on either of them.

wrong.why: two workings that each ran without a hitch look like two ways of doing one job, and the chapter has already shown a fraction and a decimal being two ways of writing one amount.
wrong.move: decides both answers must be right in their own way, since each lane followed a rule it was given.
wrong.screen: the question the fraction asked is read out again at the top of the stage and both answers are held against it in turn, each one turned back into a fraction on the bench and stood beside the fraction it started from. One comes back to it and one does not, and the one that does not is left standing beside what it actually came to, with the distance bar still drawn between the two answers.

phases.screen: the same fraction loaded into both lanes with the distance bar still empty
phases.soWhat: Zeros on the left make a number smaller and zeros on the right make it bigger, and this step wants smaller.
phases.concept: Why the side matters so much

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, when the second lane is let go. The same fraction runs down both lanes at once and in step: above, the zeros walk into the empty places on the left of the digits and the point card comes in from the right hand end; below, the zeros hang themselves past the right hand end and that lane's point card comes in from the right of what they built. Both lanes reach a finished answer on the same tick and neither is marked. The distance bar then draws itself between the two answers and writes how many times apart they are, and the two sit there side by side for as long as anybody wants to look at them, with the voice saying nothing about either of them.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a fraction stands at the top with its denominator lit and the zero counter beside it empty. On the second the numerator lies out in digit cards with the point card waiting just past their right hand end and the counter already set. On the third a short numerator lies out with the counter set higher than the cards can reach, so the places still empty are drawn and lit between the point and the digits, and the zero tray stands open beneath them. On the fourth the same fraction is loaded into both lanes, the upper one worked and the lower one untouched, with the distance bar drawn empty between them. The running count at the top left holds the fractions turned against the fractions this phase lays out, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the lit denominator, or the point card at the right hand end, or the empty place nearest the point, or the untouched lower lane, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how many zeros are underneath. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any numerator over ten, a hundred or a thousand, with the zero tray, the wrong side lane and the distance bar all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on counting the zeros underneath, walking the point in from the right, filling the empty places on the left, and what the wrong side costs.
voiceLines: Count the zeros underneath first. That is how many places you are going to need.
Count the zeros underneath. That is how many places you need.
Start at the right hand end and walk the point in. Count as you go.
The digits have run out. Which side are the empty places on?
Try it the other way and see where it lands. How far apart are they?
Another fraction. Count what is underneath before you touch anything above it.
Free play. Any numerator, any of the three denominators, wrong side lane and distance bar open.
Send the point card back to the right hand end and walk it in again, counting.
Every point walked in from the right, and every filling zero standing in front of the digits.

observations.why: Each zero underneath is one more split by ten, and each split by ten is one more decimal place.
observations.soWhat: The number of decimal places comes from counting zeros, so a hundred asks for two places and not for three.
observations.observe: The counter read the zeros of the denominator, not its digits, and never showed anything else.

observations.why: The last digit of the numerator is the one that has to land in the last decimal place the denominator calls for.
observations.soWhat: The point is counted in from the right, and counting in from the left lands a digit in the ones place instead.
observations.observe: The point card always started at the right hand end of the digits and walked leftwards.

observations.why: The digits were laid from the right hand end, so the gap they left is on their left, between them and the point.
observations.soWhat: A filling zero goes in front of the digits, on the left, and never on their right hand end.
observations.observe: When the digits ran out, the places left empty were the ones nearest the point.

observations.why: Zeros hung on the right hand end make a number bigger, and the working that follows them is carried out perfectly correctly.
observations.soWhat: A neat answer arrived at from the wrong side is still the wrong answer, which is why the side is worth saying out loud.
observations.observe: The second lane reached a tidy answer that was a hundred times too big, and nothing about it looked wrong.

phases.screen: a fraction at the top with its denominator lit and the counter still empty
phases.win: the counter settles and that many empty places are drawn to the right of a point
phases.traceback: The zeros of the denominator light one at a time with the leading digit left plain, and a point is drawn with one empty place for each zero, ending on the count of places.
ladder: Count only the zeros, not the 1.
Is every digit of that number a zero?
Look under the bar, not above it.
How many zeros has the bottom got?
Light each zero below the bar.

phases.screen: the numerator laid out in digit cards with the point card at its right hand end
phases.win: the point drops on the counted digit and the decimal is read back from the point outwards
phases.traceback: A second row is laid under the child's: its point card starts at the right hand end and walks in one digit for each zero, each place numbered from the point, ending on the decimal.
ladder: Start the walk at the right end.
How far does the counter let it go?
Which end do the steps count from?
What does the places counter say?
Walk one digit in for each zero.

phases.screen: a short numerator with places still empty between it and the point
phases.win: the zeros settle in front of the digits and every place is filled from the point outwards
phases.traceback: A second row is laid beside the child's own: its point walks in from the right hand end, the empty places light between the point and the digits with a short arrow running inward, and grey zeros fill them, ending on the decimal.
ladder: Never hang a zero on the right end.
Walk on until it matches the counter.
Put the zero before the digits.
Walk in: what is left empty?
Fill the places nearest the point.

phases.screen: the same fraction loaded into both lanes with the distance bar still empty
phases.win: both answers stand together and the distance bar says how many times out the wrong one is
phases.traceback: The other lane runs to its finish, the top lane is built with its zeros on the left of the digits, and the distance bar writes how many times apart they are, ending on the decimal.
ladder: Count the places in the lower lane.
Which side got that lane's zeros?
The counter holds a single place.
Is that the same size as the fraction?
Walk the top point in, then read it.

model.fillingZerosGo: left of the digits, between them and the point

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The zeros of the denominator light one at a time with the leading digit left plain, and a point is drawn with one empty place for each zero, ending on the count of places.
Phase 2: A second row is laid under the child's: its point card starts at the right hand end and walks in one digit for each zero, each place numbered from the point, ending on the decimal.

Phase 3: A second row is laid beside the child's own: its point walks in from the right hand end, the empty places light between the point and the digits with a short arrow running inward, and grey zeros fill them, ending on the decimal.
Phase 4: The other lane runs to its finish, the top lane is built with its zeros on the left of the digits, and the distance bar writes how many times apart they are, ending on the decimal.

voice.opening: Count the zeros underneath first. That is how many places you are going to need.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play: tap the top or bottom number to change it, then walk, fill and run.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs, shown at once UNDER the pinned instruction and kept until the child acts again
voice.onFinish: Every point walked in from the right, and every filling zero standing in front of the digits.
voice.rules: Silent: nothing is spoken (no device speech, no recorded clips, no Tap to start cover). The speech bubble is the guide: every instruction and hint is one printed page, numbers as words. The lesson is action-driven in every mode: a guide step's instruction stays until the child does the act it names; a wrong act shows that step's hint under the pinned instruction, a wrong answer the next rung of its ladder, and the hint stays unchanged until the child acts again; a right answer's next question, a phase's next phase and the summary's rows follow by themselves after a short celebration. The header's Hint key shows the step's hint or the next rung on demand. What is heard is sound effects (Web Audio), switched by the sound button, on in every mode. In classroom mode nothing waits for a tap except the pieces of a long line (the blinking arrow; a tap, Enter, Space, ArrowRight or PageDown on the bubble shows the next piece), and a tap on the bubble when nothing waits is the teacher's skip.

guide.playsOn: guide steps on phase 1, 2, 3, 4: the phase opens on its first instruction and waits for the child's act (getState guideStep, guideSteps, guideOn); the agent's check() performs the current step; the last act opens the first question. Other phases open on their printed teach lines, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

items.planQuestion: How many decimal places does 356/100 need, and how do you know? Write the decimal as well.

question.en: Count the zeros and type how many.

items.planAnswer: Two decimal places, because the hundred underneath has two zeros, and the decimal is 3.56

items.planQuestion: How many decimal places does a denominator of a thousand call for?

question.en: Now count for this bottom number.

items.planAnswer: Three, one for each zero in the thousand

items.planQuestion: How many zeros are in the denominator of 29/10, and how many digits go after the point?

question.en: Count again and type the number.

items.planAnswer: One zero, so one digit goes after the point

question.en: Walk the point in, then type it.
Now turn this one into a decimal.
Walk it in as far as the counter says.

items.planQuestion: Write 3/100 as a decimal, and say where the filling zero goes.

question.en: Walk the point in, then fill any empty place.

items.planAnswer: 0.03, with the zero placed in front of the three

items.planQuestion: Write 5/100 as a decimal, and say which side the filling zero goes on.

question.en: Walk it in and fill what is empty.

items.planAnswer: 0.05, and the zero goes on the left, in front of the five

question.en: Walk the point in, then write the decimal.

items.planQuestion: A child turns 6/1000 into a decimal by hanging three zeros on the right hand end of the six and then counting three digits in from the right. What do they get, and what should it be?

question.en: Run the lower lane, then type the right decimal.

items.planAnswer: They get 6, which is a thousand times too big. The answer is 0.006

items.planQuestion: A child writes 4/100 as 4.00 by hanging the zeros on the right hand end of the four. How far out is that, and what is the right answer?

question.en: Run it and build the top lane.

items.planAnswer: It is a hundred times too big. The right answer is 0.04, with one zero placed in front of the four

items.planQuestion: Turmeric powder is sold as 5/10 of a kilogram. Write that weight as a decimal, and say why no zero has to go in front of the five.

question.en: Write this turmeric weight as a decimal.

items.planAnswer: 0.5 kg, because only one decimal place is wanted and the five fills it on its own

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page (a tool with nextKey, runtime r48+: in user mode it waits for the child's blinking Next key instead, after every question and every phase, and the last phase's key opens the summary; AI mode, and a host that mounts one phase without navigableDots, walk on by themselves); finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

onProgress.done: questions right so far in this phase

hostContract.emits: every event is dispatched on window and, when framed, posted to window.parent as { type: 'event', name, detail }

phases.concept: Placing the point from the right
